concept.name: Load Balancing & Consistent Hashing
concept.tagline: Distribute incoming network traffic across server pools using Round-Robin and Consistent Hashing rings.

spark.summary: Load balancing is the architectural discipline of distributing incoming network and application traffic across a pool of healthy backend servers to ensure high availability, prevent server saturation, and eliminate single points of failure. By decoupling client entry points from backend execution nodes, load balancers allow systems to scale horizontally from tens of requests to millions of requests per second.
spark.keyTakeaway: Select your load balancing tier with operational intent: Layer 4 (Transport/TCP) for raw packet throughput without TLS termination overhead; Layer 7 (Application/HTTP) for intelligent path routing, header inspection, and canary splitting; and Consistent Hashing when routing stateful connections or cache-sensitive requests.

concept.whyItMatters: A single server, no matter how powerful, has finite hardware boundaries (CPU cores, RAM bandwidth, socket descriptors, network interface card saturation) and represents a catastrophic single point of failure. Load balancers distribute requests across N redundant instances, continuously probing backend health to automatically steer traffic away from degraded or failed nodes before users experience errors.
whenToUse: Scaling web applications, APIs, and microservices horizontally across multiple compute instances.
Distributing traffic across multiple Availability Zones (AZs) for high availability and disaster resilience.
Terminating TLS/SSL certificates and offloading cryptographic handshake overhead from backend application workers.
Executing zero-downtime progressive deployments (Canary, Blue-Green, Rolling updates) via weighted traffic shifting.
Preserving cache locality or WebSocket connection affinity across stateful backend worker pools.
whenNotToUse: Single-instance internal development tools or batch jobs where high availability and horizontal scaling are unnecessary.
Ultra-low-latency financial trading applications where an intermediate network hop introduces unacceptable microsecond latency (use direct client-side routing instead).
Monolithic architectures running in-memory session state that cannot be replicated or distributed across multiple servers.
When upstream clients can natively execute deterministic client-side load balancing via service mesh (e.g. gRPC Finagle/Envoy).
keyPoints: Layer 4 (L4) Transport Load Balancing: Operates at the TCP/UDP layer (IP:Port), routing raw packets without decrypting TLS or inspecting HTTP headers. Delivers extreme throughput (> 1,000,000 packets/sec) with minimal CPU overhead.

Layer 7 (L7) Application Load Balancing: Operates at the HTTP/gRPC layer, terminating TLS and inspecting request paths, headers, and cookies to enable content-based routing (e.g. routing /checkout to payment pods and /catalog to browsing pods).

Health Check Probes (Active vs Passive): Active health checks send periodic synthetic HTTP GET /healthz requests; passive health checks observe live client traffic to eject nodes returning repeated 5xx errors.
Dynamic Balancing Algorithms: Round Robin, Weighted Round Robin, Least Connections, Weighted Response Time, and Consistent Hashing with virtual nodes.
Direct Server Return (DSR): Advanced L4 optimization where requests route through the load balancer, but backend servers respond directly to clients, bypassing the LB return bottleneck.

examples.title: Layer 7 Path-Based Microservice Ingress
examples.scenario: An e-commerce platform routes incoming mobile app traffic to specialized microservice clusters based on HTTP request URI paths.
examples.outcome: Requests to /api/v1/orders route to high-memory transactional pods, while /images/* routes to an edge CDN cache, isolating critical checkout from static assets.

examples.title: Consistent Hashing Cache Cluster Routing
examples.scenario: A distributed caching layer with 20 Memcached nodes routes keys based on consistent hashing.
examples.outcome: When a cache node fails, only 1/20th of the cached keys are remapped to new nodes, preventing a catastrophic database cache stampede.

tradeOffs.pro: Layer 4 handles millions of packets per second with negligible CPU usage because it does not parse application protocols.
tradeOffs.con: Layer 4 cannot inspect HTTP paths, cookies, or headers, preventing intelligent content routing, WAF inspection, or canary traffic splitting.

tradeOffs.factor: Centralized Hardware/Cloud LB vs Client-Side Load Balancing
tradeOffs.pro: Centralized LBs (AWS ALB, F5, NGINX) decouple clients completely from backend topology changes and IP addresses.
tradeOffs.con: Centralized LBs add an extra network roundtrip hop (1-3 ms) and introduce an expensive centralized infrastructure dependency.

tradeOffs.factor: Least Connections vs Consistent Hashing Distribution
tradeOffs.pro: Least Connections dynamically balances load across heterogeneous servers, preventing slow requests from backing up.
tradeOffs.con: Least Connections scatters requests randomly across nodes, destroying local in-memory CPU and application cache hit rates.

failureModes.name: The Thundering Herd Health Check Recovery Storm
failureModes.description: When an overloaded backend node recovers from a crash, the load balancer detects it as healthy and instantly dumps thousands of queued connections onto it, crashing it again.
failureModes.mitigation: Implement Slow-Start traffic ramping (warming period) where traffic increases gradually (10% -> 50% -> 100% over 2 minutes) rather than instantaneously.

failureModes.name: Zombie Node Routing due to Flaky Health Checks
failureModes.description: A backend server returns 200 OK on /healthz because the health endpoint is a static dummy, while application worker threads are locked in database deadlocks.
failureModes.mitigation: Implement deep health checks that actively test database connectivity, thread pool queue depth, and memory headroom before reporting healthy status.

failureModes.name: Session Affinity (Sticky Cookie) Polarization
failureModes.description: A load balancer pins clients to specific servers using sticky session cookies. A few high-volume users end up pinned to the same backend host, causing CPU exhaustion while other nodes sit idle.
failureModes.mitigation: Migrate to external stateless session storage (Redis/DynamoDB) and eliminate sticky session dependencies in favor of pure Least Connections routing.

commonMistakes: Using simple Round Robin when request processing times vary by orders of magnitude (e.g. 5ms search vs 10s report export), which overwhelms unlucky nodes.
Failing to configure connection draining (graceful shutdown timeouts) when terminating or updating backend instances, severing active client TCP connections.
Placing single load balancer instances in front of production systems without Multi-AZ Active-Passive failover or DNS Anycast redundancy.

deepDive.markdownContent:
## 📖 Operational Architecture of Modern Load Balancing

In high-scale distributed architectures, load balancing is the critical bridge between untrusted, unpredictable public network traffic and resilient backend compute clusters. A load balancer functions as an authoritative reverse proxy, accepting client connections at an edge IP and intelligently forwarding packets or requests to a pool of backend servers.

```architecture
{
  "view": "high-level",
  "title": "Layer 4 & Layer 7 Multi-Tier Load Balancing Architecture",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "clients", "label": "Client Traffic (Anycast IP / DNS)", "type": "client" },
    { "id": "l4", "label": "Layer 4 LB (ECMP / Maglev / IPVS)", "type": "route" },
    { "id": "l7", "label": "Layer 7 Ingress (Envoy / NGINX / ALB)", "type": "gateway" },
    { "id": "appA", "label": "Service Pool A (Checkout / Payment)", "type": "service" },
    { "id": "appB", "label": "Service Pool B (Catalog / Browsing)", "type": "service" },
    { "id": "telemetry", "label": "Observability (Prometheus / Datadog)", "type": "pulse" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "clients", "to": "l4", "label": "Raw TCP SYN Packets (1,000,000 rps)" },
    { "from": "l4", "to": "l7", "label": "Distributed TCP Streams" },
    { "from": "l7", "to": "appA", "label": "HTTP/2 /checkout (Path-Routed)" },
    { "from": "l7", "to": "appB", "label": "HTTP/2 /catalog (Path-Routed)" },
    { "from": "l7", "to": "telemetry", "label": "Latency & Error Telemetry" }
  ]
}
```

---

### ⚙️ Layer 4 vs Layer 7: Operational Comparison

| Dimension | Layer 4 (Transport / TCP/UDP) | Layer 7 (Application / HTTP/gRPC) |
|---|---|---|
| **Protocol Awareness** | IP addresses, TCP/UDP ports, TCP sequence numbers. | HTTP verbs, URI paths, headers, cookies, JSON payloads. |
| **Throughput / Scale** | Extremely High ($10\text{M}+$ packets/sec on commodity hardware). | High ($50\text{k} - 200\text{k}$ requests/sec per multi-core node). |
| **TLS/SSL Handshake** | Passes encrypted packets directly to backends (or terminates via specialized TLS offloaders). | Fully terminates TLS, decrypts payload, inspects HTTP content, re-encrypts to upstream. |
| **Routing Capability** | IP hash, 5-tuple hash (`src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port, protocol`). | Path routing (`/api/v1`), header routing (`Host: beta.example.com`), cookie session affinity. |
| **Resource Cost** | Minimal CPU & Memory footprint (packet forwarding). | High CPU overhead for TLS decryption, gzip decompression, and header parsing. |
| **Typical Tools** | Linux IPVS, AWS NLB, Google Maglev, HAProxy TCP mode. | Envoy, NGINX, AWS ALB, Traefik, HAProxy HTTP mode. |

---

### 📊 Observability Coverage: Key Metrics & Alerting Thresholds

Operating a production load balancer fleet requires rigorous monitoring across the Four Golden Signals:

#### 1. Traffic & Throughput
- **Active Connection Count**: Real-time count of open client and backend TCP sockets. A sudden drop signals edge network cuts; a runaway spike indicates connection leaking.
- **Request Rate (RPS)**: Ingress HTTP requests per second broken down by protocol (HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 vs gRPC).

#### 2. Latency Histograms
- **Time to First Byte (TTFB)**: Measures the delay between the client sending the request and the LB forwarding the first byte of backend response.
- **Target Response Time (p95 / p99)**: Backend processing duration. A divergence between p50 and p99 indicates backend thread starvation or slow database locks.

#### 3. Error Rates & Anomalies
- **HTTP 502 Bad Gateway**: The load balancer received an invalid response, connection reset, or TCP RST from the backend pod.
- **HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout**: The backend server accepted the connection but failed to complete the request within the configured proxy timeout window (e.g. 30 seconds).
- **Backend Healthy Host Count Percentage**: $\frac{\text{Healthy Hosts}}{\text{Total Registered Hosts}} \times 100\%$. If healthy hosts drop below $75\%$, trigger high-priority alerts.

---

### 🔄 Dynamic Load Balancing Algorithms in Practice

```text
1. Round Robin:
   Request 1 -> Node A, Request 2 -> Node B, Request 3 -> Node C
   Ideal when: All backend instances have identical CPU/RAM and all requests take equal processing time.

2. Weighted Least Connections:
   Assigns request to the node with lowest active connection count divided by its allocated weight.
   Ideal when: Long-lived connections (e.g. WebSockets, large file downloads) or heterogeneous instance types.

3. Consistent Hashing with Virtual Nodes:
   Hashes request key (e.g. User ID) onto a 360-degree hash ring with 256 virtual nodes per physical host.
   Ideal when: Routing cache-dependent requests to maximize in-memory cache hit rates without hotspotting.
```

---

### 🛡️ Step-by-Step Health Check & Eviction Lifecycle

1. **Active Probing**: Every 5 seconds, LB worker threads send an HTTP `GET /healthz` probe to each registered backend instance.
2. **Consecutive Failure Detection**: If a node fails 3 consecutive health checks (e.g. returns HTTP 500 or times out after 2 seconds), it transitions to **DEGRADED**.
3. **Immediate Traffic Severance**: The load balancer removes the degraded host from the active routing table within milliseconds.
4. **Connection Draining (Deregistration Delay)**: Existing inflight connections on the degraded node are granted a grace period (e.g. 60 seconds) to complete before TCP sockets are forcefully closed.
5. **Slow-Start Traffic Reintroduction**: When the node passes 3 consecutive healthy checks, traffic is ramped up smoothly (10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) to prevent the thundering herd from overwhelming cold CPU caches.

questions.title: Consistent Hashing Node Membership Changes
questions.prompt: What is the primary advantage of Consistent Hashing over standard modulo hashing (hash(K) mod N) when scaling cache cluster nodes?

options.text: It encrypts cache keys using AES-256 before hashing.
options.explanation: Consistent hashing is an allocation algorithm, not encryption.

options.text: Adding or removing a node only remaps K/N keys rather than invalidating almost all cached keys across the entire cluster.
options.explanation: Correct! Only 1/N keys are remapped on cluster membership changes.

rubric.excellent: Identifies minimal key remapping (K/N keys) and prevention of cache stampede on node scale events.
rubric.gap: Confuses hashing with encryption.

questions.sampleSolution: Consistent hashing minimizes key remapping during node additions/removals, re-allocating only K/N keys.
questions.explanation: Standard modulo hashing remaps ~100% of keys when N changes, causing massive cache invalidation.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Use Layer 4 Maglev consistent hashing for incoming TCP WebSocket handshakes. Use virtual nodes (vnodes=256) per voice server to evenly distribute connections and ensure scaling up or down only migrates 1/N connections.
commonPitfalls: Using simple round-robin which breaks sticky WebSocket sessions.
